responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character21_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
*settling into the conversation with a thoughtful expression*

You know, Character21_F always talked about fairness in very practical terms - it wasn't some abstract concept to her. She'd say fairness meant everyone who works hard should have a real shot at making it, but she also knew the system doesn't always work that way. Having grown up in our community, she saw how some families - including her own - had to fight twice as hard for half as much.

When it came to belonging, she had this deep connection to her neighborhood, to the families who'd been here for generations. She'd talk about how her abuela used to say "este es nuestro lugar" - this is our place. But she also understood what it felt like to sometimes be treated like you don't quite belong in your own country, you know? That experience of being questioned or looked at sideways even when your roots run deep.

Community was everything to her. She believed in people looking out for each other, especially when times got tough. She'd always say "we take care of our own," but her definition of "our own" was pretty wide - it included anyone who was genuinely trying to build something here, anyone who respected the neighborhood and contributed to it.

What stood out most was how she balanced pride in her heritage with this fierce loyalty to her community. She wanted fairness, but she also wanted to protect what her family had worked so hard to build here.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character21_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
*looking around the community garden with a mix of familiarity and contemplation*

You know, I've been in this neighborhood for decades, and I've seen it change so much. When I sit here in the garden, I see Mrs. Chen tending her vegetables - she's been here almost as long as I have, and we don't speak the same language, but we share seeds and she always waves. That feels right to me.

But then I also see... well, there's complexity here. I have no problem with people from different places - mi familia came from somewhere else too, generations back. What matters to me is whether people are trying to be part of this community or just passing through it.

The young couple from Ethiopia who moved in last year? They introduced themselves, they keep their place nice, their kids play with the neighborhood kids. That's community. But there's also people who seem to keep to themselves, or who don't seem to understand how things work here - like leaving trash out on the wrong day, or playing music too loud late at night.

I guess what I'm saying is, it's not about where you're from or what you look like. It's about respect. Do you care about this place? Are you invested in making it better? Because this neighborhood, it's been built by working families over decades. We've all had to earn our place here, and I expect the same from newcomers.

*pausing thoughtfully*

I want everyone to feel welcome, but I also want them to understand what makes this place special.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
*shifting in my seat, choosing words carefully*

Mira, I've lived long enough to know that life is complicated, and people face all kinds of struggles. My own family has dealt with addiction - my nephew went through a rough patch with drinking, and it nearly tore us apart. But we didn't give up on him because he's family.

When it comes to the neighborhood, I think there's a difference between someone's private life and how it affects the community. Two women living together, or a couple who isn't married? That's their business, not mine. As long as they're good neighbors, I don't see why that matters. Same with people from different countries or religions - I've learned more about Ramadan from my Muslim neighbors than I ever knew before.

But when someone's problems start affecting others... *pauses* Like when Mr. Rodriguez was drinking heavy and his yard became a mess, or when people were afraid to walk past his house because he'd be yelling at all hours. That's when the community has to step in, not to judge, but to help if we can.

The thing about diseases - that scares people, I'll be honest. But most of the time it's fear from not understanding. We need more information, not less communication. When there was that HIV scare years back, people were terrified until we learned the facts.

*leaning forward slightly*

I guess what I'm saying is, tolerance works both ways. I'll respect your way of life if you respect that we've built something here together. We can talk through almost anything if people are willing to listen to each other.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character21_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
*taking a deep breath, this clearly hitting close to home*

This is where it gets really hard, you know? Because I understand both sides in a way that maybe other people don't.

My family has been here for three generations, but we remember what it was like to be the newcomers. My grandfather worked construction, sent money back to Mexico, did whatever it took. So when I see people coming here looking for work, I get it. I really do.

But... *pausing, looking troubled* I also see what's happening to people in my own community. My son-in-law was laid off from the warehouse because they could hire people for less money. My neighbor's daughter, she's got her high school diploma but can't find anything that pays enough to move out of her parents' house. These are good people, people who've been here, who've paid their dues.

I think fairness means we take care of the people who are already here first - not because they're better people, but because that's what any community should do. You help your own family before you help the neighbors, right? But that doesn't mean you ignore people who are struggling.

*leaning forward intensely*

What bothers me is when employers use immigration to drive down wages for everybody. They pit us against each other instead of paying fair wages. If someone comes here legally, follows the rules, and there's work available that Americans don't want or can't fill, then okay. But it shouldn't be a race to the bottom where everyone suffers except the bosses.

The balance? Legal processes, fair wages for everyone, and jobs for people who are already here first.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character21_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
*rubbing my temples, clearly wrestling with the complexity*

Ay, this is exactly what keeps me up at night sometimes. Because when you look at it nationally, there's truth in almost all of these arguments, and that's what makes it so frustrating.

The labor shortage thing? I see it with my own eyes. The restaurant where my daughter works, they can't find enough cooks. The nursing homes are desperate for workers. So yes, there are jobs that need filling. But I also know that some of those jobs used to pay better before they became "jobs Americans won't do."

Cultural diversity... *shrugging* look, I love that my grandkids are learning about different foods and traditions. It makes them more open-minded than I was at their age. That's good.

But the security concerns? I can't just dismiss them. After 9/11, after what we've seen... I don't think everyone who worries about this is racist. Some of us just want to know who's coming in. My family came here legally, went through the process. Why shouldn't everyone?

*voice getting more passionate*

The humanitarian part, that touches my heart. When I see those families at the border with children... But I also think, what about the families already here who are struggling? Why does it sometimes feel like we care more about people coming in than the people who are already here and barely making it?

*pausing thoughtfully*

What I need is real numbers, not just emotions on either side. How many jobs are really available? What's the actual impact on wages? Are the crime statistics real or just fear? Because right now, it feels like everyone's just shouting their feelings instead of looking at facts.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character21_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*leaning back, hands clasped, speaking with the weight of lived experience*

Complete openness? No, that's not realistic. I'm sorry, but any country needs to know who's coming in and why. That's not being mean, that's being responsible. Even my own house has a front door with a lock.

Refusing everyone? That's not who we are either. This country was built by people looking for better lives, including my own family.

*sitting forward, more engaged*

I think it has to be a combination - mostly based on job demand, but with limits that make sense. Here's what I mean: if there are real jobs that employers can prove they can't fill with people already here, and they're willing to pay fair wages for those jobs, then okay. But there has to be a cap so communities aren't overwhelmed.

And it has to be legal and organized. People should apply, get background checks, have a path to follow. My grandfather waited in line, learned English, became a citizen. That process meant something to him - it made him feel like he truly belonged here.

*voice getting firmer*

But here's the key part - the people who hire immigrants have to pay the same wages they'd pay anyone else. No undercutting. And there should be support for the communities where people settle, not just "good luck figuring it out."

*pausing, then continuing with conviction*

I want fairness for everyone - for the families already struggling here, and for people who want to build a better life. But fairness doesn't mean chaos. It means having rules that work for everyone and sticking to them. That's how you build trust, and without trust, you don't have community.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character21_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character21_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
*taking a moment to transition, speaking now as J, with visible emotion*

You know... that was harder than I expected it to be. Channeling her voice like that, I could almost feel her sitting here with us.

What struck me most was how much her views came from a place of genuine care - for her family, her community, for people who are struggling. I always knew she wasn't coming from a place of hate, but doing this really highlighted how much her perspective was shaped by watching her own people work so hard just to get by.

*pausing thoughtfully*

I think I understand better now why she sometimes seemed conflicted about immigration. She genuinely empathized with people seeking better lives - how could she not, given her family's story? But she also saw the real impacts in her neighborhood, the way economic pressures were affecting people she'd known for decades.

As for my own views... *sighing* I realize I sometimes dismissed her concerns too quickly. I focused on the moral arguments about helping people, but I didn't always listen to her lived experience of seeing wages stagnate, seeing young people in her community struggle to find decent work.

*looking directly at you*

She taught me that you can care about fairness and still want systems that work. That wanting legal processes and community stability doesn't make you heartless. I wish I'd had more conversations like this with her when she was still here - really listening instead of just waiting for my turn to argue.

*voice softening*

Thank you for letting me do this. It feels like I got to talk with her one more time.
